transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas urged the U.N. General Assembly to help save a two-state
solution by preserving the land where a Palestinian state should be.
He spoke via video since the U.S. refused him a visa.
Israel's prime minister did get to deliver his address in person, as NPR's Michelle Kellerman
reports.
Dozens of diplomats walked out of the General Assembly Hall as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
came to the podium while his supporters cheered from the public gallery.
"If there are any other moral cowards who haven't yet left this hall, please do so now.
Thank you very much."
He went on to defend the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran, calling it one of the easiest
decisions he's ever had to make.
In what sounded like a campaign speech, he said Israel has hammered Hamas in Gaza and
pummeled Hezbollah in Lebanon, and he blasted his many critics here, saying they're telling
lies when they accuse Israel of genocide.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, The United Nations.
"The Navy says eight sailors attempted suicide during the 10-month tour of the USS Abraham
Lincoln Carrier Group, and PR's Quill Lawrence reports the ships are an en route home from
the Middle East."
Family members of U.S. sailors first warned about conditions on the aircraft carrier during
what became a modern record for days at sea.
At the time, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth dismissed the reports, and President Trump
said the ship's tour had been "not nearly long enough."
But in a letter responding to New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, the Navy revealed that
eight sailors had attempted suicide during the deployment, including one who jumped overboard.
Gillibrand accused the president of treating the sailors with open disrespect.
CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper has said that the Lincoln had a relatively low rate
of mental health cases, but acknowledged the stress of such a long time at sea.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
Mortgage rates are above 7 percent for the first time since January 2025, according to
Freddie Mac.
NPR's Steve Bassaha says unease, and the bond market is driving up the cost of long-term
loans.
The cost of a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has been rising fast, as investors worry about
inflation and the possibility of other interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.
Mr. O'Connor with the Mortgage Bankers Association says that really slows down the housing market.
"If they want to buy, that adds a lot to their monthly payment, also prevents some
borrowers from qualifying for their mortgage because of this higher expected payment."
Adding to the problem, high rates can trap existing homeowners where they are, which
limits supply.
Mortgage rates have risen more than a full percentage point since March.
For a new loan on a median-priced home, that's enough to increase monthly payments by hundreds
of dollars.
Steven Bassaha, NPR News.
U.S. stock indexes ended roughly back where they started after an up-and-down day.
The S&P 500 was virtually unchanged.
The Dow dropped three-tenths of a percent.
This is NPR News.
More than 83 tons of meat are being recalled across the country because the products were
not properly inspected by federal authorities and were shipped out with false inspection
stickers.
The Department of Agriculture says that the nationwide recall impacts more than 167 thousand
pounds of raw pork, beef and goat produced by Star Meat Delivery, Inc. of North Carolina.
Greece's prime minister is renewing his calls for Britain to return the Parthenon marbles.
Those are ancient Greek sculptures the British took from the Acropolis in the early 19th
century, and appears Lauren Freyer reports from London.
In a Guardian newspaper op-ed, the Greek prime minister says there is political will for the
return of the Parthenon marbles, which are also sometimes called the Elgin marbles, named
after Lord Elgin, who had them chiseled off the Parthenon more than 200 years ago.
They're currently on display in the British Museum in London.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsutakos compares the marbles to the Baya Tapestry, which France
returned to England for the first time in more than 900 years.
But unlike the Tapestry, which is back only on loan, Mitsutaka says Greece will not borrow
its own antiquities.
And he says that just as Britain would never cut the Tapestry in two, the marbles should
not be separated, as they currently are, about half in London, half in Athens.
Lauren Freyer, NPR News, London.
The sun is setting on the Connecticut WNBA franchise.
The Connecticut sun will play its final game in the state before it moves to Houston next
year.
It's the first independently owned team, the WNBA, that moved from Orlando to Connecticut
in 2003, and it was the first team to turn a profit in the league's history.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas urges UN to preserve land for two-state solution via video
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses UN General Assembly as diplomats walk out
Eight sailors attempted suicide during USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Group's 10-month Middle East deployment
Mortgage rates rise above 7 percent for first time since January 2025, Freddie Mac reports
U.S. stock indexes end roughly flat after volatile trading; S&P 500 virtually unchanged
USDA recalls over 83 tons of meat from Star Meat Delivery due to false inspection stickers
Greek Prime Minister renews calls for Britain to return Parthenon marbles from British Museum
Connecticut Sun plays final WNBA game in state before relocating to Houston next year
